#2177. England boss Thomas Tuchel angry at being dragged into race row after being told by Luis de la Fuente: 'There is no racism in Spain!' on eve of Nations League showdown

By OLIVER HOLT, CHIEF SPORTS WRITER and CRAIG HOPE, CHIEF FOOTBALL REPORTER

Published: 16:03 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 16:48 EST, 14 November 2026

Thomas Tuchel was dragged into a bitter race row on the eve of England's Nations League showdown with Spain.

Tuchel had been asked before England's departure for Spain about England's protocols in case their players suffered racist abuse at the Metropolitano Stadium on Sunday evening.

England players were notoriously subject to racial abuse at the Bernabeu in 2004 and England have not played in Madrid since.

But Spain manager Luis de la Fuente reacted angrily when he was told that Tuchel had addressed the subject.

'Tell Tuchel that there is no racism in Spain,' de la Fuente said. 'Just like in England. We are not racist.'

The row then deepened when a Spanish journalist told Tuchel about De La Fuente's reaction and the England coach grew exasperated with the line of questioning.

Tuchel had been asked before England's departure for Spain about England's protocols

'Tell Tuchel that there is no racism in Spain,' de la Fuente said. 'Just like in England. We are not racist.'

'I was polite enough to answer a question from your colleagues,' Tuchel said, 'and you run and ask Spain's coach and tell them that I talked about racism in Spain.

'I never talked about racism in Spain. I answered a question politely. I never expect racism. The dressing room is the most anti-racist place in the world. This is a perfect example of how you create confusion out of nothing.'

Tuchel had earlier said: 'It's important that the players know about the protocol. And then, yeah, we will give our answers if stuff like this happens. Best answers are on the pitch.

'We had a same discussion before the Serbia game [in Belgrade in September 2025]. There is a protocol in place.'

England midfielder Declan Rice said that Tuchel had not yet addressed the group about racism protocols but that they were clear about what they would do if any England players were abused.

England's game against Bulgaria in Sofia in 2019 was halted after allegations of racism against England players but the game was completed.

Thomas Tuchel has revealed that James Trafford will face world champions Spain on Sunday night, raising questions over Jordan Pickford’s status as England’s No 1.

It was assumed that Pickford, who the head coach maintains is his first choice, would keep the jersey given the identity of the opposition and the chance for England to top their Nations League group with victory here in Madrid.

However, Tuchel will hand Leeds stopper Trafford his fifth cap at the Metropolitano Stadium.

’We want to try and see how far Traff is,’ said Tuchel, who rotated his keepers during last month’s international break. ‘So he gets a highly competitive match. We had some changes in the back four in the last match (2-1 win over Croatia on Thursday), so we went for more stability and more experience with Pickers.

‘Tomorrow is a high-pressure match, on the biggest stage, and it's exactly what we need to see where we are with him (Trafford). Hopefully he's not too over-excited or overly nervous, because there's no need to be. We trust him. But it is different to play for England than to play for your club.

'To have the opportunity to play matches where it really matters is the best way to show up, and to show that you're ready.’

It was put to Tuchel that it would make more sense to play the goalkeeper he believes is his No 1 in the biggest game from this round of fixtures.

’It was the circumstances of the last match, that we had some changes in the back four, and that was the decision in the goalkeeping team,’ he said. 'Jordan is at the moment our No.1. I have a very clear picture in high-pressure moments. He played in tournaments and played for me in the World Cup.’

Meanwhile, centre back Ezri Konsa is also set to start after recovering from a knee issue.

‘I’m very pleased with how he has fitted in seamlessly at Arsenal,’ said Tuchel. ‘It just looks like he's always been there. For us, it’s amazing that he plays on the highest level, competes for every title, is in an atmosphere and in a situation where it really matters that you stay focused and you show up every three days. It's only positives for us.’

PROBABLE ENGLAND XI: Trafford; White, Quansah, Konsa, Hall; Anderson, Rice; Rogers, Jude Bellingham, Gordon; Kane

#2176. De Laurentiis: “Film sul Centenario? De Giovanni ha scritto la sceneggiatura, Amazon lo porterà nel mondo

Aurelio De Laurentiis, presidente del Napoli, è stato tra i protagonisti della prima edizione del premio “Eccellenza Calcistica Italiana”, manifestazione dedicata alle personalità che si sono distinte nel panorama calcistico nazionale. L’evento si è svolto a Villa Campolieto, a Ercolano, dove il patron azzurro ha ricevuto un riconoscimento nella categoria Fair Play, che vedeva tra i finalisti anche Andrea Belotti e Luca Percassi. Nel corso del suo intervento, De Laurentiis ha parlato anche del film dedicato al Centenario del Napoli: “La sceneggiatura del film del centenario la scrive il qui presente Maurizio de Giovanni. Il calcio in Inghilterra è nato con gli aristocratici. Non era un fatto popolare. Arrivarono a Napoli e iniziarono a giocare con gli scugnizzi. Il 1922 sembrerebbe la vera data, poi procrastinata al 1926 per la nascita del Napoli. Che non si chiama Società Sportiva, ma Calcio Napoli. Questo film è venuto talmente bene che una piattaforma importante come Amazon lo porterà nel mondo. Quando abbiamo vinto lo Scudetto con Conte, ho fatto un film e sono andato a Los Angeles: presi questo cinema e ho fatto questa anteprima dove sono arrivati questi tifosi dall’America. C’erano donne emozionatissime che dicevano di non capire nulla di calcio ma che si sono comunque fatte trascinare. Ho scoperto che a San Pedro ci sono 30mila tifosi del Napoli legati all’isola d’Ischia”.

#2175. Lazio, Oddo racconta Gattuso: «Rino rieducava senza mai punire»

L’ex giocatore ricorda i rimproveri nello spogliatoio del Milan e gli scherzi organizzati con Pirlo.

Massimo Oddo indica in Gennaro Gattuso il principale artefice del primato della Lazio in Serie A. L’ex giocatore biancoceleste e del Milan ha parlato del rapporto con l’amico ed ex compagno di squadra in un’intervista a Repubblica. Oltre al giudizio sull’attuale allenatore della Lazio, ha ricordato il ruolo che aveva nello spogliatoio rossonero e alcuni episodi vissuti insieme.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

Secondo Oddo, l’esperienza da commissario tecnico della Nazionale, conclusa senza la qualificazione ai Mondiali, ha inciso sulla consapevolezza di Gattuso. Non ne avrebbe però cambiato il modo di essere: «Gattuso non cambia, migliora. Da ct, mancando la qualificazione ai Mondiali, ha subito una delle lezioni sportive più grandi della sua carriera, non solo per il risultato. Adesso ha preso ancora più consapevolezza di prima».

Oddo riconosce nell’allenatore della Lazio un ruolo che aveva già ai tempi del Milan: «ma è sempre stato un “braccio armato” pronto a intervenire e risolvere i momenti di crisi. Già ai tempi del Milan. Rino rieducava senza mai punire». Il richiamo arrivava anche per piccoli ritardi e, nel suo racconto, non richiedeva l’intervento del club.

L’ex compagno precisa: «bastavano due minuti di ritardo – capitava soprattutto ai brasiliani, esclusi Dida e Kakà – e scattava il rimprovero. Non serviva l’intervento della società».

#2173. Welshman and Premier League coach among two early contenders to replace Vitor Matos as Swansea City boss

Swansea City saw head coach Vitor Matos’ departure confirmed on Wednesday. The Portuguese boss has left to take charge of RC Strasbourg, with the Swans receiving a compensation fee of around £5m and placing Leon Britton, Kris O’Leary and potentially Ashley Williams in charge on an interim basis.

The hunt for Matos’ replacement is on, and talkSPORT reporter Alex Crook states Welsh boss Rob Edwards and Liverpool first-team coach Tommy Elphick are contenders. The fresh news comes after reputable fanzine the Swansea Independent stated early talks with Edwards were held, and Elphick would be ‘open to discussions’.

Edwards is out of work and would not require compensation. Elphick’s role in Andoni Iraola’s backroom staff at Anfield means the Swans would have to pay a fee to bring him to South Wales if they wish.

Edwards and Elphick are two intriguing candidates in Swansea City’s search for a boss.

Of the two, Edwards is the most obvious. The Welshman is experienced at Championship level from his spells with Watford, Luton Town and Middlesbrough, and he has promotion pedigree to his name from his time with the Hatters. He had Boro flying too, before an ultimately ill-fated move to Wolves.

Like Matos, he favours high-intensity football, and his use of wide players at Luton Town could see him use the Swans’ squad effectively.

At the other end of the spectrum, Elphick has no senior management experience. He has emerged as a highly regarded coach since retiring in 2021, starting out in the Bournemouth youth setup before stepping into the senior side with Gary O’Neill and retaining his role after Andoni Iraola’s arrival.

Iraola took him to Liverpool with him in the summer. The fact he has never been the lead man in the dugout means we can’t know what to expect from his tactical plan, but if his principles are aligned with Iraola’s, expect fast ball progression and aggressive pressing.

Swansea City will be frustrated to lose another manager, just as they started to really build to something special. The same thing happened when Russell Martin was poached by Southampton.

The Swans made great strides under Matos’ lead, so ideally they need a head coach who will oversee a similar tactical plan. It will help them work well with the existing squad and should limit teething problems after an unforeseen change in the dugout.

Swansea City will be carefully weighing up a number of candidates but there will be an eagerness to replace Matos as soon and efficiently as possible to limit how much it disrupts their season.

#2172. Luke Graham seizes his chance to shine in Scotland back-line... now Stoke defender aims to make himself a fixture for years to come

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:01 EST, 14 November 2026

Whatever concerns there may legitimately be about the limited progress seen in Sebastien Pocognoli’s brief time in charge of Scotland, the Belgian has hardly been blessed with good fortune.

In five matches to date in the Nations League, the manager has not yet been able to select the same back-three in two consecutive outings. Injuries and suspensions have seen to that.

For all that, you sense that even if he’d had a full quota of players to choose from, Pocognoli would still be figuring out his preferred defensive grouping.

This does feel like a time of opportunity for those who are fresh on the scene. Catch the eye and there’s a real chance to become established as a mainstay of the team moving forward.

Luke Graham did his chances of doing just that no harm at all in his first start and second cap for his country on Friday.

Playing in between Ryan Porteous and Kieran Tierney, the Stoke City man made a compelling case to stay there with a strong and diligent display.

Luke Graham enjoyed a composed debut for Scotland as they recorded a much-needed win

On the back of a summer move from Dundee to the English Championship, Graham appears to have taken the step-up to international level in his stride.

‘It’s something I’ve always wanted to do since I was growing up, so I have to be ready for the moment and take it when it comes,’ he said.

‘I think there’s good competition. We have a lot of good centre-halves. Obviously, it was unfortunate for Welshy (Stephen Welsh) and Binksy (Luis Binks) to go out with injury, but that opens up a space for me to come in and try to cement a place.

‘When you’re out on that pitch, you have to do everything you can to try and stay in the team. I gave my all and I’ll just need to wait and see what happens going forward.’

Timing can be vital in football. And it’s conceivable that Graham’s might just propel him to become a Scotland regular.

While playing at Dens Park saw him mentioned in dispatches with regards to a call-up, his move to England, coming just before Pocognoli was announced as Steve Clarke’s successor, has seen his dream quickly become reality.

‘I’ve always said that one thing I wanted to do in my career was play for Scotland, so to get it over the line was pretty special,’ he reflected.

Former Dundee defender Graham proudly belts out the national anthem ahead of kick-off

‘Not much is going wrong for me at the moment, so it’s just about maintaining that and keeping it going every week.

‘I wouldn’t say I merited a start as we have a lot of good players in the camp. It’s up to the manager to pick the team and, luckily, he gave me the chance.

‘He just said to go out and enjoy it and do what you’re doing every week at Stoke. I think I did all right.’

Notwithstanding how limited the North Macedonians were on the night, Pocognoli was entitled to take encouragement from the way the back three acquitted themselves.

Playing closer to each other than we’d seen in the previous matches, they were rarely unpicked by balls through the middle. Angus Gunn was not overworked in goal. Tellingly, the only concession of the night came when Scott McTominay lost his man at a corner.

‘I think a lot of it is just being brave,’ Graham reflected. ‘It’s about bravery in going man-to-man with the striker, being brave on the ball, trying to break the lines and keeping possession.

‘So, I think bravery is the main thing and concentration as well.’

Graham keeps a close eye on North Macedonian danger man Elmin Rastoder at Hampden

With the defence solid enough, Pocognoli had a platform for a much-needed win. While the narrow scoreline made the final moments more anxious than they should have been, on balance, Scotland were deserved winners.

‘It’s just about winning games at this stage of the competition, so that was good,’ said Graham. ‘I think, if I’m being harsh, we should have killed the game off before it got to 1-1. We had a few good chances to put them to bed.

‘Then we kinda shot ourselves in the foot by conceding from a set piece. But Ben Gannon-Doak does well for the penalty and for us to go 2-1 up and see it out was good.’

No one would dispute that the display was a long way from perfect. There’s significant room for improvement ahead of the concluding group match with Switzerland on Monday.

‘We’re going through a bit of a transitional spell at the minute, so it’s not going to be all smooth sailing from the get-go,’ Graham said. ‘It’s about adjusting and trying to build on performances in every game. I think it’s going to take time.

‘It’s a different style, a different manager and we just have to keep being patient. You look at the squad now and there’s a lot of new, young players coming through. It’s just about encouraging us young boys and showing we can get a place in the squad.

‘It is going to take time but, once we get there, we’re going to do really well and compete right at the top of the game.’

Graham has been a huge success in Stoke's flying start to the Championship season

Graham does look like he’s moving in the right direction. From watching Scotland compete at the World Cup on licensed premises five months ago, he hopes he too can be the toast of the nation one day.

‘I didn’t go. It was too expensive for me,’ he explained. ‘I think I was just like everyone else, watching in the pub with their mates. It was pretty amazing and hopefully I can be part of something like that one day.

‘I wasn’t too far away (previously), I think. Steve Clarke, the former manager, told me that. It’s just about trusting myself now and hopefully getting there one day.

‘There’s been a lot of hard work and dedication which has led me to this point. I’m very grateful to a lot of people who have helped me in my career so far and just to get this chance is amazing.’

#2171. Da GTA al calciomercato, i colpi annunciati con lo stile del videogioco: c'è anche un ex Serie A

L'uscita di GTA VI riporta sotto i riflettori un universo che da sempre influenza anche la cultura popolare, compreso il mondo del calcio. Negli anni, diversi club hanno dimostrato di conoscere molto bene l'immaginario della saga Rockstar, utilizzandolo per presentare nuovi acquisti e costruire contenuti social capaci di attirare l'attenzione. Perché, nel calcio contemporaneo, un trasferimento non si racconta più soltanto con una fotografia e una maglia: serve una storia da condividere.

Nel maggio 2021 il Wisła Płock celebrò il rinnovo del difensore Piotr Tomasik con un filmato intitolato "GTA: Wisła Płock". Il giocatore entrava nel negozio del club, sceglieva il proprio outfit come in un menu, firmava il contratto e si allontanava a bordo di un'auto societaria. Pochi mesi dopo il Real Betis utilizzò un'idea simile per annunciare il ritorno di Germán Pezzella: nel video Aitor Ruibal riceveva una missione e consegnava la maglia al nuovo compagno, con tanto di messaggio "Mission Passed".

Questi contenuti dimostrano quanto il calcio abbia imparato a parlare la lingua della cultura pop. La forza non sta soltanto nella citazione, ma nella ricostruzione dei dettagli: interfacce, movenze dei personaggi e piccoli particolari riconoscibili dai giocatori. Così un'operazione di mercato diventa una storia da guardare e condividere. Nel giorno del lancio di GTA VI, quei video tornano d'attualità e sembrano un precedente per i social dei club.

#2169. Raffaele De Leonardis: “La Zes, il laghetto, le fake news: tutti i retroscena della trattativa con De Laurentiis per il centro sportivo a Qualiano”

A Radio Napoli Centrale, nel corso di Un Calcio alla Radio è intervenuto Raffaele De Leonardis (sindaco di Qualiano): “Quali sono i progetti da affiancare al centro sportivo del Napoli? Dopo la firma ho già pensato a cosa fare attorno alla zona. Quella sarà una cittadella dello sport, perché affianco ai terreni dove sorgerà il centro sportivo c’è uno stadio, ci sono campi da tennis e abbiamo in animo un palazzetto dello sport e una piscina. Oggi c’è la parte più difficile, quella della burocrazia e infrastrutture. In poco tempo che mi rimane come sindaco mi metterò a disposizione. Quante volte è saltata la trattativa con il Napoli e perché? La prima volta è saltata per il prezzo d’acquisto. Il Presidente De Laurentiis doveva valutare l’investimento. I primi terreni con destinazione urbanistica si parlava di 100 euro a metro quadro. Non c’era bisogno della Zes. Servivano 20 milioni di euro. Non era nelle disponibilità e intenzioni della società. Perché poi bisognava costruire il centro. E comparando con il Viola Park, finanziato dal 20% del Coni, ci fu un primo stop. Successivamente, la Zes paventava di superare vincoli urbanistici, allora si è cominciato a parlare di terreni agricoli. E quindi si è riallacciato il rapporto perché c’erano terreni che rientravano nei desideri della SSC Napoli. C’è stata una visita, sotto la pioggia, il famoso 30 marzo dell’anno dello Scudetto. Il Presidente del Napoli mi invitò allo stadio Maradona, vidi Massimo Boldi, c’era Serena Brancale, c’era De Martino. Quanti vaffa mi sono preso dal Presidente? Abbastanza (sorride ndr). Nell’ultima riunione c’era Chiavelli, c’erano Testa, Discepolo, c’era anche Edo e lì ho capito che forse c’eravamo. Se De Laurentiis si è messo in auto per vedere le distanze dalle stazioni ai terreni? Sì, la prima volta che venne a visitare i terreni prima di Napoli-Milan fece questo percorso in auto. Il Presidente De Laurentiis chiedeva quanto distasse dalla stazione di Afragola, ed erano circa 20 minuti, dalla stazione di Ponte Riccio al centro sono 10 minuti a piedi e da Varcaturo o zone residenziali dei giocatori sono 8 minuti di auto e dallo stadio sono 20 minuti con la tangenziale. Dall’aeroporto ancora meno, 12-13 minuti. De Laurentiis percepiva che la posizione era buona. Fece però un passo indietro in merito alla storia dei rifiuti tossici, si era spaventato, ma non era vero.

Quanto mi hanno dato fastidio le fake news attorno a questo? No, sono il Sindaco di Qualiano, ne sento tante. Però penso che ci sono solo pensieri in negativo. Ma pensiamo anche in positivo. Tutte queste problematiche potrebbero nascere, magari con la Zes. Ma noi che ci guadagniamo? Niente! C’è uno strumento di legge, sono stati fatti i migliori investimenti, noi stiamo sperando che non venga approvato? De Laurentiis ha firmato un atto notarile, un preliminare condizionato e se arriva l’autorizzazione, si trasforma automaticamente in definitivo. Lui che se ne fa di un terreno agricolo!? La Zes ha sette linee guida. Una delle linee riguarda l’attività produttiva per quanto riguarda turismo e sport. Noi non ci opporremo, perché sarebbe da folli. Chiederemo le infrastrutture che dovranno essere realizzate e aiuteremo il Napoli a realizzarle. Noi stiamo rispettando la legge. Se il prof Discepolo presenta il progetto definitivo in 10-15 giorni e partono i 90 giorni della Zes, seguiremo il countdown. Sentivo parlare di un’autorizzazione preliminare per il muro di cinta, con autorizzazione dei proprietari. Se ci sarà un laghetto? Non so se è un vezzo, ma servirà per irrigare i campi. Sarà a mo’ di cisterna. Se ci saranno hotel? Ci saranno sicuramente le stanze per i giocatori. De Laurentiis tiene tanto alla cantera, penso che farà anche un convitto per i giovani”.

#2168. Significant Leicester City ownership update emerges after being listed for £200m in August

Leicester City have had financial problems for some time now, and discontent towards long-term owners King Power has grown amid the club’s 10-year slide from Premier League champions to League One. As a result of growing unrest and dire finances, LCFC were put up for sale in August.

Now though, after limited progress and minimal news, The Telegraph has reported that the Foxes are no longer up for sale. Senior staff in Leicestershire have been informed by the Thai leadership that the club is off the market with the full focus on winning League One promotion.

Despite their debt, the club were valued at £200m upon being listed for sale. This valuation and the owners’ refusal to lower their asking price has proven a major stumbling block, and now there will be no takeover at the King Power Stadium.

Chairman Aiyawatt Srivaddhanaprabha was reluctant to list Leicester City for sale in the first place. He and the King Power ownership have consistently expressed a desire to lead the club back from their poor position and to their previous heights.

However, being put up for sale and entertaining takeover bids indicated that the ownership had realised they had done all they could to try and salvage the club to no avail. But, with a £200m valuation and tremendous debts, LCFC have proven a hard sell – despite their modern training ground and stature.

It means the supporters will have to stick it out with the current hierarchy for some time yet. The chairman and his close affiliate Jon Rudkin have been heavily scrutinised in recent years, but despite a shuffle in the boardroom and the appointment of James McCarron as sporting director, much of the day-to-day responsibility still lays with ‘Top’ and Rudkin.

No takeover means no new money for the Foxes. The financial hole they have dug for themselves will only get deeper.

As of the most recently published accounts, Leicester City have averaged losses of £60m per year for the past three seasons. Past accounts showed their debt sat at a monstrous £163m.

Now, LCFC are without the Premier League riches, and revenue on the whole will decrease drastically while they stay in League One. To find some sort of salvation without a takeover, the Foxes simply have to be successful on the pitch.

An extended stint in League One will only see them burn a deeper hole in their pockets, and it will be increasingly more difficult to clamber out of it.

#2167. Pavlovic scherza su Conceiçao: "Tolse la Nutella, aveva metodi hitleriani". Poi esalta Amorim

Strahinja Pavlovic ha raccontato alcuni curiosi retroscena sui suoi ultimi allenatori durante una lunga intervista al podcast serbo SS Calcio. Il difensore del Milan si è soffermato soprattutto sull'esperienza vissuta con Sergio Conceiçao, descrivendo un tecnico molto rigoroso nelle regole e nella disciplina, senza però risparmiare anche parole di stima nei suoi confronti.

Parlando della sua alimentazione, Pavlovic ha rivelato che, nonostante una genetica favorevole gli permetta di concedersi spesso pizza e hamburger, nei giorni che precedono le partite segue una dieta rigidissima a base di pasta, pollo e miele. Proprio su questo tema è emerso un aneddoto legato a Conceiçao: "Quando è arrivato mi ha tolto la Nutella e da quel momento non è più ricomparsa", ha raccontato sorridendo. Poi la battuta che ha fatto discutere: "Gli voglio bene, è una brava persona, ma aveva davvero metodi hitleriani".

Il centrale serbo ha spiegato che l'allenatore imponeva regole molto severe: parastinchi e gomitiere obbligatori anche in allenamento, "con temperature da o a 35°", cene separate dal resto dello staff e divieto assoluto di uscire nei due giorni e mezzo precedenti alle gare. "Cinque o sei giocatori andarono a un concerto fino alle 23. Non fecero nulla di male, ma lui lo scoprì e nella partita successiva li lasciò tutti fuori".

"Lavorare con Allegri è stato molto utile per me. È sotto la sua guida che ho fatto i maggiori progressi da quando sono arrivato in Italia. Come difensore ho una buona velocità, forza e capacità di uscire palla al piede. Sono in grado anche di lanciarmi in avanti e di segnare, ma l’aspetto tattico è sempre stato una mia lacuna. Ho imparato solo le basi quando sono arrivato in prima squadra al Partizan. Per come vedono il calcio gli italiani ero un po' in ritardo, dato che i loro giocatori iniziano ad apprendere certi concetti fin da giovanissimi".

Pavlovic ha poi elogiato l'attuale allenatore Ruben Amorim, sottolineando soprattutto la sua capacità di valorizzare i giocatori. Il difensore ha citato il rilancio di Yunus Musah, finito ai margini dopo un difficile periodo con Conceição e oggi protagonista anche in ruoli diversi. Secondo il serbo, il Milan è cresciuto anche sul piano tattico: "Con Amorim controlliamo molto di più le partite e subiamo meno ripartenze. Stiamo ancora migliorando, ma la direzione è quella giusta".

#2166. Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli urges Ben Gannon-Doak to improve his end product but insists he's happy with progress of mercurial winger

Published: 17:31 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:01 EST, 14 November 2026

Sebastien Pocognoli has backed Ben Gannon-Doak to find his killer instinct in the final third and establish himself as Scotland’s main man.

The Bournemouth youngster had an up-and-down evening in Friday’s 2-1 Nations League win over North Macedonia, getting into numerous promising positions on the right flank and winning the penalty – dispatched by John McGinn – which decided the game.

But, as has been the case throughout his Scotland career, the 21-year-old’s final ball in key moments left a lot to be desired.

Pocognoli is under no illusions that Gannon-Doak still has plenty to improve on, but insists that it won’t be long before things start to click for the talented youngster.

‘As long as he is high on the pitch and is creating one v ones I am happy,’ said the Belgian. ‘With Ben, we know that he is at a young age and needs to work on specific things.

‘On Friday, he had great opportunities. We know that he needs to improve on the end product, but he created a penalty and against Slovenia and North Macedonia away he created a number of unbelievable one v ones.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli greets Ben Gannon-Doak as he is substituted at Hampden

‘He did that last night as well. We know he can be good if we dominate the game and he can get in good positions if we control the ball. I am happy with his performance.

‘He is a young lad, just 21. Okay, he has become more mature than he was, but I believe in one moment he will have a click about decision making.

‘I believe if he is playing every game he can make many decisions. He will know that in the next game he will have to do it again.

‘If he knows that he only has to play a game every two weeks, sometimes he can think, “This is my moment”.

‘It is a process. He will become older and at some point will become relaxed in his decision making, but at this very young age what he is producing is very good.

‘I say exactly the same thing to him after training on the pitch. I say, “Ben, this is the next step”. He knows that and it is important he knows that.’

Scotland conclude their Nations League campaign in Switzerland on Monday knowing that only a victory against the group winners will be enough if they are to have any chance of leapfrogging Slovenia – currently one point better off ahead of their trip to North Macedonia – into second spot.

Pocognoli admits Gannon-Doak's end product has to improve after another frustrating show

Should that happen, Scotland would have a crack at earning promotion to League A via a play-off in March, and also crucially guarantee their place as a Pot 2 side for the upcoming Euro 2028 qualifying draw.

‘We are still alive in this competition,’ said Pocognoli, who celebrated his first win at Hampden on Friday at the third time of asking. ‘We know we have to do more than this competition. This competition is about trying to build something.

‘But it is nice to have that possibility on Monday to try to create something against one of the top 20 teams in the world.

‘We need to try to be brave. Switzerland have already qualified so let’s go there and be smart because they are a good team.

‘It is part of the process to play away against a top team. That is not something we have done yet. The approach will be different and, for me as a coach, it is a game with a lot of responsibility.’

#2165. Lazio, forza del gruppo, Dele-Bashiru: "Quest'anno siamo molto più uniti"

Il centrocampista parla del buon avvio di stagione e del clima nel gruppo.

Fisayo Dele-Bashiru è stato intervistato ai microfoni di Lazio Style Channel al rientro dagli impegni con la Nazionale, in vista della sfida di sabato tra Lazio e Lecce. Nel confronto racconta l'energia portata da Gattuso, la concorrenza interna e la voglia di dare il massimo per la squadra.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

Sto bene. Sono felice di essere tornato a Roma. Naturalmente, essere convocato in Nazionale è sempre un momento speciale, soprattutto in occasione delle qualificazioni alla Coppa d'Africa. Le partite sono andate abbastanza bene. La prima è stata positiva, la seconda poteva andare meglio, ma sono felice di essere tornato a Roma. Nel fine settimana ci aspetta una partita importante e non vediamo l'ora di giocarla.

Penso che quest'anno abbiamo iniziato molto bene con Gattuso. Ha portato nuova energia nello spogliatoio e credo che questo si veda nei rapporti tra i compagni, nel nostro rapporto con l'allenatore e anche in quello con i tifosi. Se riusciremo a continuare su questa strada, sarà perfetto.

Tanto, in questo momento c'è molta concorrenza. Quando ho l'opportunità di entrare in campo per aiutare la squadra, cerco sempre di dare il massimo. Se dovessi giocare nel fine settimana, darò come sempre tutto me stesso. Credo che questo sia importante perché, per arrivare lontano in campionato, non bisogna poter contare soltanto sugli undici titolari: anche i giocatori in panchina devono dare il proprio contributo. È fondamentale.

Credo che la concorrenza sia sicuramente positiva e faccia bene. Tutte le migliori squadre del mondo hanno molta competizione interna e penso che questo permetta alla squadra di esprimere al meglio. In questo momento l'atmosfera è molto buona. Credo che nello spogliatoio ci siano molte più battute e momenti di leggerezza rispetto alla scorsa stagione, quando la situazione era differente. Quest'anno siamo molto più uniti e questo contribuisce sicuramente a creare un bel clima all'interno del gruppo.

Da quando sono alla Lazio ho avuto diversi allenatori. Credo che quest'anno un aspetto importante sia il grande coinvolgimento di Gattuso nel lavoro con il gruppo e con ogni singolo giocatore. Ha un ottimo rapporto con tutti i componenti della squadra e penso che questo sia fondamentale. Inoltre, sa perfettamente cosa significhi essere in campo ai massimi livelli, avendo avuto una grande carriera da calciatore. È un allenatore di altissimo livello, tutti i ragazzi gli vogliono bene e dobbiamo continuare a ottenere risultati per lui.

A livello personale sono una persona piuttosto tranquilla. Non lascio che quello che succede all'esterno influenzi troppo il mio modo di essere. Penso di comportarmi in campo proprio come nella vita di tutti i giorni: sono abbastanza rilassato e calmo, anche se so essere aggressivo quando serve. Direi che queste sono le caratteristiche che mi descrivono meglio.

A livello personale, il mio obiettivo è giocare il maggior numero possibile di partite e aiutare la squadra il più possibile, magari con gol e assist. Se riuscirò a fare tutto questo, penso che sarà una stagione davvero molto positiva, non soltanto per me, ma anche per tutti i ragazzi. Adesso dobbiamo semplicemente continuare a lavorare partita dopo partita. Speriamo di riuscire a proseguire su questa buona strada.

#2162. Out-of-form West Ham man set to keep starting berth vs Preston North End with potential replacement ‘struggling’

West Ham goalkeeper Mads Hermansen has been under fire recently, with poor performances prompting calls for Alphonse Areola to be brought into the starting XI. However, the Frenchman suffered an injury in the warm-up before WHUFC’s defeat to Blackburn Rovers before the break, ruling him out.

And, after the international break, doubts remain over Areola’s availability. Speaking to the official club media ahead of Saturday’s clash with Preston North End, Scott Parker said: “We’re struggling a bit with Alphonse at the moment. He probably looks a bit unlikely. We’ll probably leave it as late as we can to see if he’s fit to be involved.”

Elsewhere, Max Kilman is suspended, but Kyle Walker-Peters could be in line for a return. Parker made no mention of the full-back in his pre-match interview, saying: “There’s nothing really jumping out, other than Alphonse.”

Areola isn’t ruled out of West Ham’s clash with Preston North End, but it would be a surprise to see him start. If Parker goes into the weekend planning to start the Frenchman and it transpires that he isn’t ready to go on matchday, it throws that section of the pre-match preparations out of the window.

Despite his struggle for form, it is smarter to prepare for the game with Hermansen in goal. That will frustrate some sections of the WHUFC support, but it is the sensible move to make.

Hermansen has started every Championship game this season, but his performances have been far from convincing.

He isn’t solely responsible for the underwhelming defensive record of four clean sheets and 24 goals conceded in 16 games across all competitions. However, the Dane’s displays have left a lot to be desired with an inability to command his box and errors when coming to claim crosses leading to chances for the opposition.

Given his form, a fully fit Areola may have got the nod. For this weekend though, it seems Hermansen will keep his place.

When Areola is at 100%, Hermansen will have a fight on his hands to keep his place.

It means that if he does start again against Preston North End as expected, he needs to put in a far more assured performance. A clean sheet would not go amiss, but the most important thing is to act with confidence and conviction. If he can command his box, comfortably claim crosses and show composure on the ball, it will go a long way to easing concerns around his form.

If not, Areola will be waiting in the wings to come into the WHUFC side when fit. If his absence extends longer, then youngster Finlay Herrick may be considered if Parker feels a chance is needed.

#2161. John McGinn warns Tartan Army it might take 18 MONTHS for Scotland to click into gear under new boss Pocognoli

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:42 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:03 EST, 14 November 2026

Amid the clamour for a change at the helm following another poor showing at a major tournament, it was easy to lose sight of the reality of the situation.

Steve Clarke didn’t crash and burn in the US because a raft of world-class talents failed to turn up on the biggest stage. It happened primarily because a limited squad was unable to outperform two top-ten nations in Brazil and Morocco who could call upon infinitely superior footballers.

Sebastian Pocognoli has since arrived on the scene having earned a stellar reputation from his title success with Union Saint-Gilloise and his less feted spell at Monaco. But he has not come armed with a magic wand.

In opening the door to a string of fresh faces and advocating the more attacking approach which so many craved, the turbulence he’s experienced to date should only have been expected.

Limited by both the standard of players who are eligible for Scotland and the time he has to work with them, only the blissfully naïve would have seen his appointment as a quick fix.

While there were some positives to be taken from the game with North Macedonia – primarily the result – it’s likely the nation will have to endure more short-term pain for long-term gain.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli greets his players after a satisfactory evening at Hampden

This was always going to take time, perhaps, in the view of John McGinn, more than many may have imagined.

‘The manager’s got a great reputation, a good record at both places he’s been,’ said the Aston Villa captain. ‘The most important thing now in football is individuals don’t win you games. It’s unity, teamwork and everyone being on the same page.

‘You see how successful clubs and successful countries do it. And we want to be one of them.

‘It’s not going to happen overnight. There’s a lot to learn but we did create big chances against North Macedonia where we could have scored three, four or five and it could be a different story.

‘But this isn’t something that gets fixed in March or even next September. It will start to build over the next 18 months.’

If that predicted time frame might raise an eyebrow or two, McGinn makes no apology for it. Call it managing expectations from the midfielder if you please. But without a degree of patience from the Tartan Army, he feels Pocognoli’s ideas won’t take root.

‘I understand it’s frustrating,’ he added. ‘It’s freezing and you want to see four, five, six goals, but the balance has got to be there.

McGinn sends his penalty home to give Scotland a deserved lead against North Macedonia

‘They’re entitled to their opinion, but there’s got to be a mixture of patience.

‘The supporters are entitled to say whatever they like. But just as long as they hurl anything they want to shout at the experienced boys and just let the young ones flourish and try and settle into the team.’

Give credit where it’s due. With Clarke accused of causing stagnation by selecting the same old faces, Pocognoli has capped five players for the first time while recalling the likes of Oli McBurnie.

The sages in the stands can’t have it both ways. If the squad was going to evolve, it was never going to be a smooth ride.

‘I think the young players are starting to show more now,’ McGinn stressed. ‘Luke Graham on Friday night, I thought he was brilliant. It’s not easy playing in the middle of a back three. He’s been waiting for his chance and the manager’s shown that if you deserve your chance you’re going to get put in there.

‘We’ve got so many players that can step up and they will. We just need to show that belief and take it to the pitch.’

Even in victory, McGinn doesn’t dispute that there is significant scope for improvement. He’s convinced, however, that this will all come good in the end.

McGinn insists it's vital the entire Scotland squad buy into the methods of manager Pocognoli

‘We need to play slightly better,’ he said. ‘We know that, but we’re going through a period which I’ve been used to at club level, a lot of changes, a lot of detail that we need to try and remember and get used to.

‘And it’s about sticking at it. We’re keen to play a style of football that’s not easy but is going to get bums off seats. It’s important that everyone believes in it because if one person drops off or doesn’t believe in it, that’s when it all starts to fall apart.’

Friday was another memorable night on a personal level for McGinn. Having broken the tension with the opener only to see North Macedonia level, he held his nerve to put Scotland back from the penalty spot.

The brace put him on 24 international goals, now within six of Denis Law and Kenny Dalglish. But all of that is for another day.

‘It feels a bit strange, but at the minute that’s gone to the back burner,’ he stressed. ‘I had a wee chat with Scott (McTominay) about the penalties. I was designated penalty taker but, to be fair, he’s not missed one I don’t think in his career.

‘So, we had a wee chat and I think we both said the most important thing was just no matter who hit it, hit the back of the net.’

McGinn is eyeing three points against Switzerland in St Gallen to close the campaign on a high

Tomorrow, the equation is clear. To finish second in the Nations League group and secure a place in pot two for the Euro draw, Scotland must beat the Swiss and hope that Slovenia don’t beat North Macedonia.

Even if everything clicks for Pocognoli’s side, it will be the tallest of orders.

‘Difficult,’ said McGinn. ‘I know they drew on Friday night (with Slovenia) but they’ve got a couple of players back that they were missing last time.

‘It is a tough one but we want to be competing against these teams away from home. It’s not going to be perfect for a while, but we’ll stick at it.’

#2159. Morresi, regista della Lazio: nel derby l'assist per il gol di Coppola

Il centrocampista classe 2011 è stato impiegato da Rughetti in tutte le partite della stagione.

Andrea Morresi è il regista del centrocampo della Lazio di Rughetti. Secondo quanto riportato da Gazzetta Regionale, Il classe 2011, arrivato dal Perugia nell’estate del 2025, gioca davanti alla difesa ed è stato impiegato dal tecnico in tutte le partite di questa stagione. Nel derby con la Roma, un suo filtrante ha messo Coppola nelle condizioni di segnare il gol del momentaneo 2-1.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

Morresi era approdato nella capitale nella passata stagione, entrando nell’Under 15. Si è preso presto le chiavi della mediana biancoceleste, interpretando il ruolo di playmaker anche nel campionato attuale. La sua presenza è un punto fermo nelle scelte di Rughetti.

Prima del passaggio al Perugia, Morresi è cresciuto nel settore giovanile della Treiese, dai Piccoli Amici ai Pulcini. L’arrivo alla Lazio nell’estate del 2025 ha aperto una nuova tappa del suo percorso: con la maglia biancoceleste ha trovato spazio stabilmente davanti alla difesa.

In quella posizione gestisce il pallone, distribuisce il gioco e cerca gli spazi per i compagni. Alla visione di gioco unisce tecnica e corsa nelle due fasi. Il suo destro si è già fatto notare anche sui calci di punizione, una soluzione con cui può rendersi decisivo.

Il suo contributo non si esaurisce però nella regia arretrata. Quando si apre la possibilità, Morresi avanza verso la trequarti avversaria. È dunque coinvolto sia nella costruzione delle azioni sia nel lavoro che precede le iniziative offensive della squadra.

Fino alla domenica del derby, la Lazio condivideva con la Roma l’imbattibilità in campionato. I biancocelesti si presentavano alla sfida con una struttura difensiva che li rendeva la seconda miglior difesa del raggruppamento. Anche il lavoro di Morresi davanti alla retroguardia contribuisce all’equilibrio della squadra.

Contro i giallorossi, il numero 4 ha giocato in una zona di campo particolarmente affollata. Dall’altra parte c’era il miglior attacco del girone, capace di mettere alla prova la mediana biancoceleste. La Roma ha prevalso per 3-1 dopo aver dominato gran parte degli 80 minuti, ma nella ripresa la Lazio ha trovato la forza di reagire.

L’episodio che ha riaperto momentaneamente la partita è nato dai piedi di Morresi. Un suo passaggio filtrante ha raggiunto Coppola in posizione favorevole; il compagno ha poi mandato il pallone in rete per il 2-1. La speranza biancoceleste si è spenta con il terzo gol romanista, firmato da Abate.

#2158. Positive Sheffield Wednesday injury update emerges with 75 mins per goal star fit for Barnsley clash

Sheffield Wednesday are back in action on Friday as they face Yorkshire rivals Barnsley at Oakwell. Dave Challinor will be eager to build on his first SWFC win against Plymouth Argyle, and he’ll be helped by an improving injury picture at Hillsborough.

Speaking to the press ahead of Friday’s game, Challinor revealed that star forward Louie Barry is fit for the clash with the Tykes after making his return off the bench against Plymouth. The 23-year-old has come through another week of training scot-free, but the boss remains wary that he needs to be managed carefully after his long-term ankle injury.

Elsewhere, Ashley Maynard-Brewer and Ali Al-Hamadi have trained with no issues, and internationals Kieran Morrison, Jordi Liongola, Sean Fusire and Will Grainger returned with no injuries. With no new blows, the Owls only remain without Max Lowe, Reece James, Mason Burstow and Tyler Onyango.

Sheffield Wednesday have lacked a killer instinct in attack at times this season. The failure to convert control into goals played a part in Henrik Pedersen’s downfall, so it is down to Challinor to right the ship.

The 3-0 win over Plymouth Argyle showed big attacking improvements, and their frontline only grows stronger with Barry’s return. He is a proven star at League One level and has already shown SWFC fans how potent he can be in his limited time on the pitch since joining in the summer.

Barry’s comeback will give Challinor a welcome but tricky selection dilemma to resolve. The former Aston Villa and Barcelona prospect can play at striker or on the left-hand side, and there is strong competition for both of these positions.

Davis Keillor-Dunn‘s form has seen him solidify a place in the team, while it was Callum Slattery and Barry Bannan who played in the most advanced roles behind the number nine against Plymouth Argyle.

If Challinor is to play with a three-man frontline, Barry may be perfect for the place on the left. However, the Owls boss will have to work out who drops from the team to facilitate his inclusion.

There is an understandable eagerness to see Barry back in the first XI. He is one of League One’s standout players and has the potential to be a real star in an exciting chapter at Sheffield Wednesday.

However, Challinor is right in saying that he can only play such a role if they are smart with his return. If they rush him into too much too soon, he will be at risk of re-injury or separate setbacks.

By managing his minutes over the coming weeks, SWFC give themselves the best chance of having Barry fit and available for longer. He will be a key influence in Challinor’s attack, but only if they’re careful in the early days of his comeback.

#2156. 3 managers Blackpool must target as club legend Ian Evatt departs after 12 months

Blackpool have had a terrible start to the season which has left them just above the relegation zone after 13 games. Club legend Ian Evatt had come in last season and their was plenty of positive signs coming into this campaign but they have now come through.

As a result, Evatt has departed the club, confirmed by Blackpool on Thursday afternoon. Evatt was a crucial player for Blackpool when they went from League One to the Premier League just over a decade ago, making over 250 appearances.

Steve Thompson will take charge of the team for this weekend’s game against Wigan Athletic, along with Stephen Crainey, Stephen Dobbie and Steve Banks. The Tangerines are on the lookout for a new head coach to take them up the table.

With that said, here are 3 managers that Blackpool must consider to replace Evatt…

Gary Rowett brings substantial Championship and League One experience and a proven ability to organise and stabilise sides quickly.

During long spells at Millwall and Birmingham he regularly extracted solid results from squads that were not the strongest in the division, often through compact defensive structures, aggressive pressing and pragmatic game management.

He is tactically flexible rather than wedded to one system and has a track record of improving results mid-season. For a Blackpool side currently near the bottom of League One, his experience of grinding out points and rebuilding confidence would be a clear asset.

Luke Williams’ standout achievement was guiding Notts County to promotion from the National League with a record points total and highly attractive, possession-dominant football. However, he was dismissed by Peterborough United in League One this season.

He builds sides that control games, press effectively and score freely, which could energise the Blackpool support and improve the squad’s technical confidence. He also has experience of the demands of League One and the Championship.

Matt Bloomfield’s strongest case rests on his excellent work at Wycombe, where he turned a mid-table League One side into one of the division’s most competitive teams, regularly challenging near the top while playing energetic, high-intensity football.

He is known for his player-centred approach, clear communication and ability to create a positive culture. Although his subsequent spells at Luton and Oxford were less successful, those were at Championship level.

In League One he has shown he can overachieve with limited resources, making him an attractive option for Blackpool’s current situation. With Blackpool struggling at the moment, his player-management skills could be crucial to get the club back on track.

#2155. 'Dad, we are not walking out of the match. It's my first time in Old Trafford!' - An afternoon with my 10-year-old inside the Theatre of Screams for Carrick's last stand

Published: 18:49 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:49 EST, 14 November 2026

‘Mate, we are walking out in the 21st minute to protest 21 years of the Glazers. Will you join us?’ he asks earnestly, handing me a leaflet that announces: ‘Enough is Enough! Empty Old Trafford! Leave the stadium in the 21st minute. 21 years of failed ownership. Glazers OUT! Ineos OUT!’

More than 70,000 spectators leaving their seat and walking out of the stadium in the 21st minute have been quite the statement, especially live on Sky Sports.

But as admirable as Saeed TV’s aim is (I discover later he is some sort of youtuber), it’s hard to see gain any traction.

‘Dad, we are not walking out of the match. It’s my first time in Old Trafford,’ I am told as we continue to meander up Matt Busby Way, a declaration from my 10-year-old that causes a fair bit of mirth among the crowd.

Mate, we are walking out in the 21st minute to protest 21 years of the Glazers. Will you join us?’

‘What’s wrong with the owners anyway?’ Dan enquires innocently, which leads to a bind.

How deep down the rabbit-hole should I go with my ten-year-old on his first visit to the Theatre of Dreams.

It’s probably not the time or place to try and explain leveraged buyouts and how much debt the Glazers have saddled the club with, £1.2 billion at the last count while taking millions out of it in dividends. Do I need to go further back and talk about Rock of Gibraltar’s unexpected success on the track and the concept of stud fees?

‘They are not putting enough money into the team and taking loads of money out of the club,’ is all I offer.

‘When Manchester City need a midfielder, they can buy Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez while United have to make do with someone who was sitting on Chelsea’s bench.’

He doesn’t look convinced that’s much of a reason to walk out of a football but as the cathedral of consumerism that is the Manchester United megastore has appeared, he forgets about United’s disastrous ownership model – for now, at least.

During his doomed attempt to coax Jurgen Klopp to Old Trafford around 2014, Ed Woodward apparently told him that United was the sporting version of Disneyland.

And to be sardined inside the megastore in the couple of hours before kick-off, you have to accept that the much-maligned former CEO may have been right about one thing.

Think Arnott’s a couple of days before Christmas, just with a lot more people. You even need to pass through airport-like security before even entering and spend your dosh.

One of the common refrains among United supporters is why are the Glazers holding onto the club when they don’t even seem to care.

Thirty seconds inside the megastore on match-day and you realise why the Americans are so keen to hold onto the asset they’re bleeding dry – and they probably care a great deal.

Dan gets obligatory photo at statue of United's holy trinity, a moment he will look back on

Even with the team languishing in the relegation zone, having won a single league game all season, people are keen to spend, spend, spend.

I see people wandering around with five or six different shirts, from different eras (I did succumb and bought Dan the black shirt from 95-96 season, because it reminds me of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and better times!)

You can get a photo with a replica of a Premier League trophy. That’s just £10. Or Lego sets of Old Trafford or the Munich clock.

That will just set you back £25.  For many in this shop, it seems allowing the club to empty their wallet is as much a part of the day as the actual football.

There are other parts of the ritual, which remain and have yet to be infected by the poisonous atmosphere around the club – and remind the three dads bringing their kids to Old Trafford for the first time of better days.

Such as curry chips and battered sausage from Lou Macari’s chipper. And the customary photo in front of the statue of the holy trinity of Best, Law and Charlton.

The megastore was the one place that seemed immune to the toxicity in the air. Once outside again and all that could be heard was the moans and groans, mainly because Shea Lacey wasn’t starting.

Coming here since the 1990s, we have seen the skyline of Manchester transformed as it became a sleek, modern city. It seems the one place that hasn’t changed is Old Trafford. It has remained the same.

Stuck in time. It looked sleek and modern in 1999, but now there is a tired, decrepit feel to the stadium – and not just because of the leaking roof. It could do with a lick or two of paint.

Stuck in time. It looked sleek and modern in 1999, but now there is a tired, decrepit feel to the stadium

No wonder Big Sir Jim is determined to plough ahead with his plans to make a crudely-designed circus tent ‘the Wembley of the North.’ Not that there is anyone inside Old Trafford of the same mind.

Senne Lammens has just trotted onto the field with Tom Heaton and Karl Darlow to do their pre-match warm-up when the chants start, telling Jim Ratcliffe he can stick his new stadium up his posterior.

It is a weird atmosphere, with all the chanting against the owners – both Glazers and Ineos – and nothing being sung in support of the players.

As my friend points out it must be so difficult for the team to show the best of themselves when things are this toxic in the stadium.

Dan has been to the Jodi Stand enough times on a Friday night to know there is plenty of choice and crude language at football matches, but still I nearly felt at covering his ears at some of the stuff being sung in Old Trafford last Sunday, especially that directed at CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

We had hoped that things might have been different when the game kicked off, but within a minute, Aston Villa had scored.

And three minutes later, they had scored again when Lammens fumbled Alysson’s shot into Nicolas Jackson’s path. Maybe walking out in the 21st minute wasn’t such a bad idea.

The crowd’s ire had gone from the owners to the players now, with a sustained chant of ‘You are not fit to wear the shirt.’ United did rally and by half-time, it was 2-2. But the mood was still dismal as we queued for a quick beer.

The 1958 Group had asked fans not to buy booze, another protest against the owners. But it seemed nobody was paying much attention to that.

One of the issues at United is that there seem to be too many splintered fan groups – there is also ClaimBackUnited and Fan Coalition ’58 – as well as Saeed TV, who seemed to be on his own solo run.

We didn’t feel bad about ignoring the booze ban, as everyone was doing it. And within a couple of minutes of the second-half, we saw the reason why. You need to fortify yourself to watch Diogo Dalot try to defend.

For much of the second-half, it seemed like Michael Carrick’s brief tenure was going to peter out in a forgettable defeat, as Villa seemed to manage the game perfectly.

Dan and his friends were growing frustrated, pointing out the players weren’t doing what their coaches tell them to do on a weekly basis, leading me to conclude that maybe my son’s under-11 side are better-coached than United.

The last on-pitch act of Carrick's tenure

And then there was the chaotic and crazy final few minutes in stoppage-time. And a draw that came out of nowhere and was celebrated like a victory.

That was the thing. Even though the mood inside the stadium was toxic for most of the game, even though the team were two down inside four minutes and the season has been a disaster, everyone still came away from Old Trafford, happy and with a smile on their face.

Only football can do that. More than that, perhaps only Manchester United – despite everything – can do that.

#2154. England's Euro 2028 mission starts NOW! Thomas Tuchel's men must beat Spain to prove they can compete with the best - or risk their 'DNA' cursing them yet again, writes OLIVER HOLT

Published: 16:10 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 19:04 EST, 14 November 2026

It is four months, almost to the day, since England shrank from the call of history and lost their World Cup semi-final to Argentina in Atlanta but Thomas Tuchel may not believe that the Nations League tie against Spain in the Metropolitano on Sunday evening represents his best shot at redemption for the way things played out that afternoon in America’s South.

That is largely because Tuchel does not appear to believe he has anything to redeem himself for. The manner of his side’s capitulation - and the substitutions he made - in the Mercedes-Benz Stadium last July enraged the nation, but Tuchel said the fault was in the damned DNA of the English, that we were underlings, and that our players found it constitutionally impossible to keep hold of the ball.

Whatever Tuchel thinks, the fact remains that the tie against Lamine Yamal, Fabian Ruiz, Pedri and Mikel Oyarzabal and the rest of the world champions at the home of Atletico Madrid offers Tuchel and his players the opportunity to encourage themselves and their fans that they are not destined to be also-rans wired to fall at the final hurdle for evermore.

Spain are formidable opposition. They are on a record-breaking run of 43 matches unbeaten and have won their last 12 in succession. They haven't drawn a game since their June 15 game against Cape Verde in the World Cup. Their last defeat was on March 22, 2024, when they lost 1-0 to Colombia in a friendly. Some ask whether they are the best international side the world has ever seen.

‘Spain seem unbeatable,’ Tuchel said, when he walked into the press room at the Metropolitano on Saturday night and heard hymns of praise being lavished upon the opponents he is about to face.

‘They have a very strong identity and a very strong mentality. We are trying to take it away from them. We are up for it. We are up for the fight. We are up for a spectacular match. We can see how far we can push the limits with the world champions in Madrid. The group is full of self-belief and rightly so.’

England must beat Spain to prove they can compete with the best - even if they have flaws

Thomas Tuchel must show he can find a way around the limitations presented by the 'DNA' he has complained about

This may be the toughest game that Tuchel’s England side play until the European Championships in 2028, where the final will be contested at Wembley, and they will play all their games at home. They need to go into that tournament with the belief that they can beat the best when the pressure is at its highest.

Beating Spain away in the final game of the group phase of the Nations League is not quite the same as a critical match at a major tournament but it is as stiff a challenge as Tuchel is going to face until then. Beating Croatia 7-0 in front of gangs of schoolkids in Rijeka last month was hailed as the best England performance of the Tuchel era. Which says it all, really.

It was a great performance in a relatively meaningless match. Now it is time for him to show that he can marshal an England side to succeed against the very best, not fall apart when the prize is in sight. His protestations of powerlessness in the aftermath of the Argentina defeat were not a good look for a coach who was hired with the idea that his coaching prowess and his game management could get England over the line.

Has he learned anything from the manner of the Argentina defeat? ‘This game against Spain will be proof of concept at the highest level,’ he said, ‘but we are up for it. I think we have taken the next step after the World Cup. The best thing is to trust our process and trust ourselves. We need to be clear about how we want to impose ourselves and I think that is all visible.’

Now it is time for him to show that he can find a way past the limitations of England’s footballing DNA, find a way to compete with Spain and France when it really matters, and find a way to end the culture of near misses that has come to be England’s lot in the last decade of appearances in semi-finals and finals.

England have played six matches since that day of crushing disappointment in Atlanta and scored 22 goals. But in the only one of those matches that really mattered, they lost 3-2 to Spain at Wembley in the opening tie of their Nations League campaign at the end of September, a game in which they were largely outclassed by Luis de la Fuente’s team.

Spain are what England have to aim for. Tuchel mentioned their example and their ability and their mindset straight after the semi-final loss to Argentina. ‘Ball possession plays a crucial role,’ he said at his post-match press conference in Atlanta. ‘It’s maybe not in our DNA like it is in our Spanish DNA or in our Argentinian-Brazilian DNA, to take the ball and control the game with the ball.’

This may well be their toughest game until the final of the 2028 European Championships, if they get that far

The England coach said more recently that England need to go back to trusting a traditional style that emphasises direct, high-intensity physicality rather than trying to copy Spanish patience in ball-retention. England, though, were taught a lesson in sophistication by the Spanish in September.

And for all the attention lavished on Yamal, Spain’s defence is the best in the world. Rodri, the shield for that defence and also the world’s best in the role, is not fit for this game but even without him, Spain’s back-line inspires an awful lot more confidence than England’s.

‘They were the best in the World Cup at the back,’ Declan Rice, England’s central midfielder, said on Saturday. ‘Defence wins you titles. Everyone talks about their attacking talent but you look at their central defenders, their full backs and the way their midfielders contribute to the defence, too.’

That defence will have to stop England’s resurgent front line, led by Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane, who could be flanked by Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers and backed up by the supreme talent of Jude Bellingham just behind them.

Bellingham’s improving relationship with Tuchel, which cannot have been harmed by the inclusion of Bellingham’s brother, Jobe, in this squad, is another reason to hope that England still retain the capacity to improve after the World Cup. The elder Bellingham has become England’s most influential player.

England at their best would be one of the few teams capable of extending them. Rice said on Saturday that the game between the two sides was ‘massive’. England need to prove they can find a way to get closer to the world champions. To beat them, Rice said, would be a ‘massive statement’.

‘Playing against them is a great incentive to win. It will show where we are as a group. We are trying to attack teams full throttle and with players like Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham and Morgan Rogers in our attack, it feels as if it is going to take off one night and maybe tomorrow night will be the night. We can beat Spain. For sure, we can.’

Tuchel needs to prove England can win, not just be noble contenders. They need to prove that their DNA need not be a curse.

#2153. Red card for football chiefs as they announce ex-Premier League referee is dead aged 78 - when he is still alive and kicking

Published: 13:01 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 20:45 EST, 14 November 2026

A former Premier League referee was mistakenly declared dead by football chiefs this week.

On Tuesday, the Football Association of Wales (FAW) announced Keith Cooper had died aged 78. But he is alive and well.

The news reached the ears of the Wembley Cup final referee when he went out to his local sports centre for a flu jab only to be told: 'You were dead.'

The Football Association of Wales posted a statement online and a tribute on social media to announce his death, but then withdrew it within an hour.

Mr Cooper, who is the father of former Nottingham Forest and Leicester boss Steve Cooper, told a Welsh sports website: 'I walked into the sports centre yesterday to have my jab and the fellow went, "You were dead!"

'Well, I'm not dead, I'm here and I'm OK!'

The blunder appears to have emerged after the Wiltshire FA announced the death of another referee called Keith Cooper, who the football chiefs in Wales believed was the other Keith Cooper.

The FAW statement said: 'Keith was a well-known figure who enjoyed an exceptional career at both domestic and international level and would later hold the position of FAW Referees' Officer following his retirement in 1996.

On Tuesday, the Football Association of Wales (FAW) announced Keith Cooper had died aged 78

Mark Beeney goalkeeper of Leeds United is Sent Off of by Referee Keith A Cooper for hand ball outside the area during the Premier League match between Manchester United and Leeds United at Old Trafford on April 17, 1996 in Manchester, England

Former professional football John Fashanu is pictured with referee Keith Cooper during a Wimbledon F.C. match

'Born and raised in Pontypridd, he is considered one of Wales' best match officials through his highly-regarded status in the game.

'In addition to his work with FAW, Keith was also a valued member of the Wiltshire FA Council who recognised his 'integrity, passion and commitment' in their tribute to his services to the game.

'Everyone at the FAW sends their condolences to his family and friends at this sad time.'

Mr Cooper oversaw the 1994 League Cup final between Aston Villa and Manchester United, won by Villa 3-1, and worked in radio punditry after hanging up his whistle.

The FAW has not issued an explanation over the posted tribute. His family has not yet commented on the error.

But the unfortunate mistake has not spared the FAW from ridicule by other football fans.

One said: 'We always said there was only one Keith Cooper - turns out there are two.'

Another said: 'Glad the whistle wasn't blown too early on Keith and much respect to the family of the other one.'

#2152. Ex-Nottingham Forest, Leeds & Sunderland star lands manager's job at non-league club

Liam Bridcutt has become the latest one-time Championship player to land a job on the managerial circuit, with his appointment at Ashington AFC confirmed on Wednesday evening.

The 37-year-old was a regular fixture in English football's second tier throughout the 2010s, having initially helped Brighton and Hove Albion return to the division after a six-year absence under Gus Poyet for the 2011/12 campaign.

Bridcutt also made several appearances in League One for various clubs, as well as achieving gametime in the Premier League during a mixed spell with Sunderland.

There have been many surprise moves into the non-league game from former Championship stars in recent months.

Kyle Hudlin and Britt Assombalonga are now a strike partnership at National League South outfit, Harborough Town, all of Chey Dunkley, Ryan Woods, Marvin Johnson and Elias Kachunga linking up at Solihull Moors of the National League, whilst former Burnley and Derby County star, Jeff Hendrick has confirmed his role as ambassador at Ebbsfleet United.

Bridcutt ended his playing career two years ago, and since then has obtained coaching roles, but will now lead a side in the dugout for the very first time.

After confirming his retirement from playing in February 2024, the two-time Scotland international landed his first coaching role seven months' later by becoming a sessional coach within Newcastle United's academy setup despite his prior connections with the Magpies' bitter North East rivals.

Soon afterwards, though, Bridcutt joined another local side in the form of Gateshead, becoming assistant to Carl Magnay in October 2024, although the boss of the National League club would resign at the end of 2024/25 after missing out on a play-off spot by one point.

Just two weeks ago, the former midfielder became part of Ashington's interim management setup with Paul Dunn, having previously been an associate of head of football, Ian Skinner, during his spell at Gateshead.

The Northern Premier League Division One East side then confirmed that Bridcutt had accepted the offer of becoming permanent manager at Woodhorn Lane in midweek, with it being claimed: "The appointment represents an exciting step for Ashington AFC as the club looks ahead to the next chapter of its footballing journey."

Ashington are currently 20th in the table, inside the relegation zone, having accumulated 16 points from their opening 18 fixtures.

Many who supported clubs in the Championship within recent times are likely to have been intrigued by Ashington's managerial appointment, as Bridcutt was often credited for being underrated in his defensive midfield role for various clubs in the division.

He made 182 of his 383 career appearances in the second tier, which included guiding Brighton to the 2012/13 play-off semi-finals, where they were defeated by M23 rivals, Crystal Palace.

How underrated was Liam Bridcutt in the Championship? Comment below!

After signing for Sunderland in a £2.5m deal, Bridcutt made just 30 Premier League appearances and later returned to the Championship to turn out for the likes of Leeds, where he was appointed captain in 2016 under Garry Monk, as well as Nottingham Forest and and Blackpool.

As well as earning promotion from League One with Brighton, Bridcutt also made appearances in the third tier for Lincoln City and Bolton Wanderers, with the Imps defeated against his future employers, Blackpool, in the 2021 play-off final at Wembley.

Bridcutt is yet to speak to the media following his appointment with Ashington, but given his vast experience within the EFL and Premier League as a player and coach, he will be hoping to continue the area's proud footballing legacy.

Indeed, two of the country's most famous footballers, Sir Bobby Charlton and Jack Charlton, hailed from the Northumberland village before being a part of England's only FIFA World Cup-winning squad in 1966.

FLW ranks the eight most famous footballers to have played in the Championship at some point in their career.

It remains to be seen what the future holds for Bridcutt on the managerial circuit, but he will hope it starts with a crucial victory against Morpeth Town on Friday.

#2151. Liverpool coach joins Rob Edwards on Swansea City manager radar

Swansea City are on the hunt for a new head coach after Vitor Matos departed for Ligue 1 side Strasbourg, and both Rob Edwards and Tommy Elphick are among the contenders to replace him.

The Championship side has yet to formally announce Matos' departure, but the BlueCo-led French outfit confirmed his arrival on Wednesday, with the Swans set to receive around £5 million in compensation for his services.

Matos leaves Swansea having taken them from 20th in the second tier upon his arrival midway through last season all the way to the summit in the early stages of the ongoing campaign.

A run of four defeats in five leading up to the November international break saw them drop to sixth, but they're still three points off Birmingham City, who currently occupy the top spot.

Now, Swansea have to source someone who can maintain their strong start, as they look to mount a promotion challenge after five consecutive campaigns finishing between 10th and 15th.

According to TalkSPORT's Alex Crook, two of the early candidates to replace Vitor Matos as Swansea boss are former Wolves head coach Rob Edwards and Liverpool coach Tommy Elphick.

Edwards has been out of work since the summer, when he was rather unceremoniously sacked by Wolves following their relegation from the Premier League. He found out the news from social media while he was on holiday, after being one of the driving forces behind the signing of Kieran Trippier and the return of Raul Jimenez.

Which fanbases can improve on their current atmosphere offerings? The computer has had its say....

In the Championship, he has experience at the top end of the table. He took Luton Town up into the Premier League in the 2022/23 campaign, and last season had Middlesbrough battling amongst the automatic promotion places before leaving for Molineux.

He has had his failings at this level, though, such as with Luton following their relegation from the top flight and at Watford for a brief period in 2022, although he isn't the only manager to fall victim to the events at Vicarage Road.

Meanwhile, this isn't the first time that Elphick has been linked with a head coach role at Championship level. The former Bournemouth defender rejected the opportunity to take over at Bristol City during their managerial search during the off-season, instead following Andoni Iraola to form part of his coaching staff at Liverpool.

The 39-year-old has coached ever since his retirement in 2021, being part of the first-team staff at the Vitality Stadium since Gary O'Neil's time at the club in 2022, until he left for Anfield in the summer.

Swansea fans are still stung by Matos' departure and the haste with which it happened. Strasbourg's official approach only took place on Monday, with this whole ordeal coming quite out of the blue.

Those at the Swansea.com Stadium had become admirers of the football being played under the Portuguese boss, playing high-intensity, pressing football while also being good in possession, too. Replacing him will be difficult, and supporters online aren't enamoured by the reports linking their post with Edwards and Elphick.

The majority of the discourse is coming Edwards' way, though.

The 43-year-old isn't seen as an inspiring choice, even despite his relative success at Championship level, and some Swans fans don't think he'd be able to oversee a smooth transition from the football seen under Matos.

"Don’t particularly want us to go down the Rob Edwards route to be honest, as I’m not convinced he’s the right fit for us in terms of style of play," one fan said in response to the reports.

"If it is Rob Edwards I'd be extremely disappointed. Would undo all the good work we've done over the last year," another said, while a third commented, "It’s just so underwhelming, isn’t it?"

Even one fan commented, "Rob Edwards, no, Tommy Elphick, yes," indicating that they'd rather have someone who hasn't been a head coach yet in his career over Edwards at this stage of the season.

Swansea went against the grain and took a risk with hiring Matos back in November last year. The then-37-year-old was incredibly inexperienced as a main dugout man, taking charge of 12 games for Portuguese side Maritimo before heading to South Wales.

Especially with the club being advised by Jamestown Analytics now, the data company founded by Brighton and Hove Albion owner Tony Bloom, perhaps it should be expected that Matos' replacement will equally be out of left-field, if the data can advise manager hires, that is.
